what_its_for: Flunisolide is a steroid (corticosteroid) medicine used to help control and prevent symptoms of asthma, such as wheezing and shortness of breath. The nasal spray form is used to relieve stuffy, runny, or itchy nose caused by allergies. It works by reducing swelling and irritation in your airways or nasal passages.
how_to_take: For the inhaler: Shake well before each use. Breathe out fully, place the mouthpiece in your mouth, seal your lips around it, and breathe in slowly and deeply while pressing down on the canister. Hold your breath for about 10 seconds, then breathe out slowly. Rinse your mouth with water and spit it out after each use to help prevent a mouth infection (thrush). For the nasal spray: Blow your nose gently first. Tilt your head slightly forward and insert the tip into one nostril. Press the other nostril closed and spray while breathing in gently through the nose. Do not spray directly onto the middle wall of your nose. Use exactly as your doctor prescribed — do not use more or less than directed.
dosing: For asthma (inhaler): Adults and children 6 years and older typically use 2 puffs twice a day (morning and evening). Your doctor may adjust your dose based on how well your asthma is controlled. For nasal allergies (nasal spray): Adults usually start with 2 sprays in each nostril twice a day. Children 6 to 14 years old usually start with 1 spray in each nostril 3 times a day or 2 sprays twice a day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as doses vary by person.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not double up or take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep away from heat, direct sunlight, and open flames — the inhaler canister is pressurized and can be dangerous if exposed to high heat. Do not puncture or throw the canister into a fire. Keep the cap on the inhaler or nasal spray when not in use. Keep all medicines out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Do not use flunisolide as a rescue inhaler during a sudden asthma attack — it will not work fast enough. Always have a fast-acting (rescue) inhaler available for sudden symptoms. Avoid exposure to chickenpox or measles if you have not had them, since steroid medicines can make infections more serious. Tell your doctor right away if you are exposed. Avoid stopping this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, especially if you have been using it for a long time.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor if you notice: white patches or sores in your mouth or throat (possible yeast infection/thrush); your breathing gets worse or you need your rescue inhaler more often; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or difficulty breathing; vision problems or eye pain; unusual weight gain, swelling in the face (moon face), or stretch marks on the skin (signs of too much steroid); signs of adrenal problems such as extreme tiredness, weakness, nausea, or dizziness; nosebleeds that are frequent or severe (with nasal spray); fever, chills, or signs of infection that do not go away.
when_it_works: Flunisolide does not work right away. For asthma, it may take 1 to 2 weeks of regular use before you notice improvement in your breathing. For nasal allergies, most people begin to feel better within 1 to 2 weeks. It works best when used regularly every day, even when you feel fine. Do not stop using it just because your symptoms improve.
special_populations: Children: Flunisolide can be used in children 6 years and older, but children should be monitored closely, as long-term use of inhaled steroids may slow growth slightly. Regular check-ups with your child's doctor are important. Older adults: No special dose adjustment is usually needed, but older adults should be monitored for bone loss (osteoporosis) with long-term use. Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Talk to your doctor before using this medicine. It should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed, since uncontrolled asthma can also be harmful to your baby. It is not known if flunisolide passes into breast milk in significant amounts. People with infections: Tell your doctor if you have any current infections, especially tuberculosis (TB), fungal infections, or any untreated bacterial infections, as steroids can make infections worse.
